questions.question: Why can't a coding agent just search for what it needs?
options: It can't search for code it doesn't know exists, and reading files one by one to get oriented eats context
Search is not allowed in repos
questions.explanation: A map shows what exists and how it connects, so the agent knows where to look.

questions.question: Why does the map show signatures instead of function bodies?
options: Signatures say what's callable and how, at a fraction of the tokens; the agent reads bodies only where needed
questions.explanation: 103 tokens covered five files' interfaces in the demo; bodies would cost far more.

questions.question: What does an edge A → B mean in the lesson's graph?
options: A and B are in the same folder
File A references a name that file B defines
questions.explanation: Score flows from users to definers, so widely used code ranks high.

questions.question: For the login task, models.py still ranked first. Why?
options: Every file uses models.py, so structure keeps it high; and 'log in' in the task didn't match 'login' in the code
questions.explanation: Structural centrality and crude word matching both limit task personalisation.

questions.question: The rendered map would exceed the budget if the next file were added. What does render() do?
options: Skips that file and keeps trying smaller ones that still fit
questions.explanation: The map stays within budget while fitting as many high-ranked files as possible.

questions.question: When is a precomputed repo map most useful compared with pure search-based exploration?
options: In the first steps on an unfamiliar repo, where orientation matters most; it costs a fixed token amount every turn
Only for repos with one file
questions.explanation: Maps front-load orientation; exploration spends turns instead. Many agents combine both.
